tag: Sprint 14 Task E, F117 (F114 cloud read)

qelm-protocol-reservoir-linear-readout: Section II.A, Overview of QELMs, p.2: the paper itself describes the protocol (fixed reservoir channel into a larger Hilbert space, linear readout trained on pre-characterized states). The surrounding paragraph says the same.
qelm-training-known-states-linear-system: Section II.A, Training, p.2: W is obtained by supervised training on known states, Eq. (1) is the linear system, and the text says known states amount to a high degree of control of state preparation.
entanglement-witness-definition: Section II.A, Estimating entanglement witnesses, p.4: the paper defines the witness and the certification criterion Tr(W rho) < 0. The definition is the standard one, cited to Guhne and Toth, and the paper uses it as its own.
apparatus-two-photon-qw-oam-25-dim: Section II.B, Reservoir dynamic and measurement, p.4, with Fig. 2 and Section IV: two parallel QWs, OAM values -2..2 per photon, 25-dim walker space, then SLM projective OAM measurement. Waveplates and q-plates are named in the same section.
apparatus-photon-source-sagnac-ppktp: Section II.B, Input states preparation, p.4: SPDC in a PPKTP crystal in a Sagnac configuration; pump polarization switches separable and maximally entangled states. Fig. 2 caption agrees.
apparatus-wavelengths-and-pump: Appendix B2, Photon-pair generation, p.14: 808 nm pairs by SPDC in ppKTP, cw pump at 404 nm, Sagnac interferometer.
experiment-three-reservoir-configs-e1-e3: Section II.B, Summary of experimental settings, p.4: E1 optimized angles, E2 swaps two E1 angles, E3 uniform random angles. Appendix B3 gives R1, R2, R3 consistently.
experiment-sample-sizes-and-reference-st: Section II.B, Summary of experimental settings, p.4: 150 separable and 150 entangled for E1 and E3, 83 for E2; reference separable state VV for E1, VH for E2 and E3; the paper attributes the difference to acquisition issues. Table S2 agrees on the reference states.
noise-dataset-construction-weighted-oam: Section II.B, Effect of input states mislabeling, p.6: the noise dataset is a weighted combination of measured OAM distributions of entangled and separable states, giving rho_noise = (1-p) rho_ent + p rho_sep, in scenario E2.
shadow-tomography-values-are-lower-bound: Section II.B p.7 and Appendix D, Knowing counts vs frequencies, p.22: the authors state the shadow-tomography MSEs are lower bounds because N is unknown and they report the minimum over guessed N, which depends on the observable and is not physical. This is a caveat the paper states about its own benchmark.
shadow-tomography-detailed-model-caveat: Section II.B, Benchmark with shadow tomography, p.7: the authors state that a more detailed apparatus model could push shadow tomography beyond the QELM, and that building and validating it is time-consuming and resource-intensive. A caveat on their own benchmark.
shadow-benchmark-uses-ideal-model-of-app: Appendix D p.22 gives the effective POVM from the ideal isometry V of the two QWs and the polarization projection |eta>; Section II.A p.4 says the real apparatus deviates owing to imperfections and thermal fluctuations. Both parts are the paper's own statements of its benchmark setup.
polarization-projection-not-strict-povm: Appendix B1, Polarization projection, p.13: SLMs need fixed polarization, so the map is a non-trace-increasing CP map followed by a projective measurement, not strictly channel plus POVM; this only increases the data needed. Stated by the paper about its own apparatus.
training-state-generation-uniform-random: Appendix B3, Input states, p.15-16: uniform random waveplate angles; equal angles on both arms for E1, E2, E3, E5, E6; independent angles for E4. Table S2 agrees.
partially-entangled-dataset-sizes: Appendix C, Training with partially entangled reference states, p.19: 249 and 357 states, equally split among maximally entangled, partially entangled and separable, R2 reservoir, identical angles at state preparation.
limitation-ideal-state-prep-assumed: Section II.A, Training, p.2: training states are assumed known, which amounts to a high degree of control of state preparation, and imperfections in preparation give imperfections in the estimation.
limitation-apparatus-not-ideal: Section I, Introduction, p.1: the authors state the apparatus is not expected to be ideal because its effective measurement differs from MUBs and SIC-POVMs, and that modeling all components and noise is challenging.
limitation-statistics-and-acquisition-ti: Section II.B, Dependence of performances on reservoir configuration, p.7: E2 and E3 need additional statistics to reach the 1/N regime; the paper says longer acquisition could achieve it. The paper also states the practical 10-hour acquisition choice.
data-and-code-availability: Appendix B3 (p.15) gives the GitHub URL for reservoir values, data and code; Section V.D (p.9) says the data will be available in Zenodo. The paper's own statements of where its data and code are held, not verified here.
qw-step-structure-two-steps-per-walk: Section IV, Materials and Methods, p.8-9: two-step evolution per QW, Eq. (8), U = U1 x U2, five OAM states per photon, 25-dim space, q-plate angles fixed by fabrication.
sharma-test-sets-and-cutoff: Section 6, pp.5-6: three test sets divided by query terms, and a 5 minute cutoff per query, both stated in the experimental section.
sharma-experiment-hardware: Section 6, p.6: 4-core 3.40 GHz Intel processor with 32 GB RAM, 18,383 decision trees and ten best features, all stated in the paragraph that describes Table 3.
sharma-benchmark-selection: Section 6, p.5 and footnote 9, p.6: the two selection principles (exclude trivial queries, use real-world applications) and the note that some queries initially took over 20 minutes, all stated by the paper about its own benchmark.
sharma-baseline-ablation-design: Section 6, p.6: f(s) = w0 + w1 fDT + w2 fSL; baseline sets w1 and w2 to zero, DT row sets w2 to zero, SL row sets w1 to zero, as stated beside Table 3.
sharma-cyc-kb-size: Section 3, Background, p.2: states the KB has 21.7 million assertions and 652,037 individuals. This is a count describing the system the experiments run on, stated by Cycorp authors and not independently verified. A snapshot of the paper's date (2016).
sharma-cyc-axiom-counts: Section 3, Background, p.2: the six axiom and role counts for default inference mode are listed in one sentence. They describe the system tested, stated by Cycorp authors and not independently verified. A snapshot of the paper's date.
sharma-heuristic-module-definition: Section 3, Background, p.2: the paper defines a heuristic module as a tuple (w_i, f_i), the net score as the weighted sum, and selection of the highest-scored node.
sharma-restriction-condition-definition: Section 4, p.3: the paper defines a restriction condition x:tau and the satisfying substitution (maps x to ground term t with Sigma entailing tau(t)). The second half of the value comes from the sentence after the quoted one.
sharma-decision-tree-representation: Section 4, p.3 and Fig. 1: the constraints derive from successful uses of a rule, are represented as decision trees, and the training set is made by querying the rule antecedent for a fixed duration.
sharma-createtree-algorithm: Section 4, p.3 and Fig. 1: branching test is the most specific maximally covering generalization; AND branch for other variables, OR branch for other values; stopping rule on unexplained examples. Matches the value.
sharma-dt-insufficient-alone: Section 4, p.3: the authors say that, because the KB might have thousands of rules relevant to a query, decision trees alone are not enough and other steering is needed. It is a hedged motivation ("might") but the paper states it as a limit of the first technique; Table 3 shows DT alone gives less speedup than DT+SL on test set 1.
sharma-regression-data-collection: Section 5, p.4, Data Collection: 40 percent of nodes sampled, 46 features recorded, 2.5 million data points.
sharma-regression-target-and-transform: Section 5, p.4, Data Transformation and Learning: number of answers is the performance measure, z-score normalization, log10(1 + number of answers) target.
sharma-future-work: Section 7, Conclusion, p.7: the four future-work items are stated by the authors. The first (test on a larger query set to understand dynamics) states a scope limit of the present tests.
sharma19-mcts-ordering-heuristic: Abstract: the paper describes a search heuristic using Monte-Carlo simulation to choose inference steps and tests it on Cyc. States the paper's own method and test bed.
sharma19-key-idea-simulated-paths: Introduction: the key idea is to simulate several thousand paths from a node, and node values are the average number of answers from simulated paths through the node. The Simulation-Based Learning section gives the same method.
sharma19-all-axioms-ordering-focus: Related Work: the authors state they focus on ordering heuristics that work with all axioms, in contrast to premise selection. A statement of the paper's own scope.
sharma19-heuristic-module-definition: Background: a heuristic module is the tuple (w_i, f_i) with f_i assessing the quality of an inference step (state, action), and Cyc uses a set of modules to pick the best clause from the set of support.
sharma19-baseline-policy: Background, Eq. (1): the baseline policy pi_BASELINE is Cyc's default, built from the listed heuristics, and is called the baseline in the experiments.
sharma19-search-formulation: Background: proof search as states and actions sampled without backtracking until a terminal state with outcome z; the reasoner aims to maximize z.
sharma19-q-value-definition: Background: Q(s,a) is the value of action a in state s and is the expected reward, given by the average over simulation outcomes in the displayed formula.
sharma19-mcts-search-tree-stats: Simulation-Based Learning: the tree has a node per generated state and each state stores N(s), N(s,a) and Q(s,a) for every applicable action.
sharma19-tree-and-default-policy-phases: Simulation-Based Learning, Fig. 1 text: tree policy to depth d, default policy beyond d, outcome backed up through selected nodes.
sharma19-uct-tree-policy: Tree policy paragraph, Eq. (2): UCT builds the tree from the current state, unselected actions go first, otherwise the action maximizing Q + c sqrt(log N(s)/N(s,a)).
sharma19-exploration-parameter-c: Tree policy paragraph: c biases the search toward or against exploration, and the paper reports experiments varying c (Figs. 2-5, Table 1).
sharma19-default-policy-30s: Default policy paragraph: Cyc's existing mechanism is the default policy, run for a fixed 30 seconds.
sharma19-value-update-rule: Updating Values, Eq. (3): at a terminal state the answer count R is observed; N(s,a), N(s) and Q(s,a) are updated, with Q(s,a) moved toward R by 1/N(s,a).
sharma19-state-features-2698: Search Space Formulation: 2,698 features = 2,664 sub-type features + 33 instance features + sub-goal depth. The sum checks.
sharma19-edges-are-resolution-steps: Search Space Formulation: edges correspond to resolution steps that transform one node into another.
sharma19-tabular-no-generalization-knn: Search Space Formulation, Eq. (4): Q is a partial tabular representation, which does not generalize easily, so the paper defines a k-nearest-neighbor average with Manhattan distance.
sharma19-mcts-heuristic-module: Search Space Formulation, Eqs. (5) and (6): the module uses k-NN over the MCTS output and is used to order inference steps.
sharma19-benchmark-real-queries: Experimental Results principle (a) and footnote 7: queries came from knowledge engineers and programmers to test applications and the engine; mostly one answer expected for a fully bound query.
sharma19-four-fold-protocol: Experimental Results, footnote 9: queries split into four parts, one for test and three for training, repeated for four experiments.
sharma19-speedup-definition: Experimental Results: speedup(e) = Time(baseline, e) / Time(MCTS, e), defined by the paper in the text before Fig. 2a.
sharma19-hardware-and-cutoff: Experimental Results, after Fig. 2a: 4-core 3.40 GHz Intel, 32 GB RAM, and a 10 minute cutoff per query.
sharma19-stated-future-work-limits: Conclusions: three future-work items stated by the authors. Item (i) states that generality on a larger query set is not yet shown, a limit of the present tests.
rqg-model-setup: Abstract and Section IV (p.1, p.5): complete graphs on n vertices with an edge removed, two leads at the removed edge's vertices, transmission coefficient computed. Fig. 1 shows the model.
rqg-gilbert-model-def: Section II.B, p.2: the Gilbert G(n,p) model with edge probability p and q = 1-p; the paper says it will be employed in this work.
rqg-open-graph-setup: Section II.C, p.3: free Schrodinger operator on each edge, Neumann-Kirchhoff conditions, c semi-infinite leads for an open graph with c channels.
rqg-nk-amplitudes: Section II.C, p.3: the paper states r_i = 2/d_i - 1 and t_i = 2/d_i, independent of k, for its Neumann-Kirchhoff model. It is a standard property used in its calculations, stated without derivation, so it counts as the model setup and not as a new result.
rqg-def-exact-transmission: Definition III.1, Eq. (6), p.3: the exact transmission coefficient is the p-weighted sum over spanning quantum subgraphs of |sigma|^2, with p the randomization parameter. The formula is garbled in the text layer but the value matches the readable parts.
rqg-exact-calc-cost: Section III, p.3-4: the number of subgraphs of the complete graph is 2^(edges), and the paper says the count scales exponentially with the number of vertices and that Eq. (6) can be hard to implement. This is the paper's stated cost limit of its exact definition. The loose wording "exponentially in vertices" is the paper's; the count is 2^(n(n-1)/2).
rqg-monte-carlo-method: Section III, p.4, Eq. (7): the paper's own method, ensembles drawn uniformly at random with a fixed edge count, without repetition, counting isomorphic subgraphs separately, then averaged.
rqg-proposition-1-proof: Appendix, p.8, eqs. (A.1)-(A.4): readable in the text. Substituting Eq. (7) into Eq. (8) and taking the limit |S| -> binomial (A.2), the double sum becomes the sum over all spanning subgraphs, equal to Eq. (6). The value describes this correctly. What is proved is the limiting identity only, not the convergence claim, and the proof is a short algebraic step.
rqg-scope-limits: Section I, p.1: imperfections include damping, leakage and noise, and the paper concentrates on simple quantum graphs with random edges, which it says does not cover the many possibilities.
rqg-future-work: Section V, p.7: the randomization definition allows randomizing a chosen set of edges, and other generalizations are left to future works. States what the paper does not cover; the first clause follows from Section II.B.
sinno-scope-framework: Section I, Our Contribution, p.1: the paper introduces an embedding framework for large complete bipartite graphs on adiabatic processors, leveraging Pegasus. The word universal is the authors' label.
sinno-scope-pegasus-only-future-work: Abstract and Section VI: the benchmark is against Minorminer on Pegasus only, and future work is extension to other topologies, hybrid optimization and real workloads. The paper states these as not yet done.
sinno-def-minor-embedding: Section I (p.1) and Section III-A: minor embedding as mapping logical qubits onto chains, and G is called a graph minor of U.
sinno-def-generic-topology: Section III-B, Eq. (2), p.3: the paper defines G(M) with D = alpha M (M-1) and cells forming K_a,b, as quoted. Flag: the paper calls alpha the vertex degree, but for Pegasus it writes D = 12M(M-1) with nominal length 12 and degree 15, and later calls alpha the nominal length. The definition is the paper's own but is internally inconsistent.
sinno-def-coordinates-labelling: Section III-B, Eq. (3), p.3: qubit (u,w,k,z) with u = 0 vertical and u = 1 horizontal, offsets w, k, z, and the integer label z + (M-1)(k + alpha(w + M u)). Matches the value.
sinno-algorithm-mapping-equations: Section III-B, Eqs. (4)-(6), p.4: the cell count and the visible-to-horizontal and hidden-to-vertical mappings. Eq. (4) is a flattened fraction in the text layer; its vertical layout (V above min(m,n)) fits Hv = V / min(m,n), consistent with Eq. (7) using V mod min(m,n). The value flags the flattening.
sinno-algorithm-overflow-case: Section III-B, Eq. (7), p.4: for V > min(m,n)M the extra cells are Hv,add = V mod min(m,n), with the two start ids given by Eq. (3) with the stated replacements. Note the paper writes the replacement tuple in the order (u,z,k,w).
sinno-setup-m4-n8-8x16-example: Section IV, p.5: m = 4 and n = 8 for Pegasus with l = 12, an 8x16 RBM as the worked example, and qubit 180 mapped to visible node 0.
sinno-method-benchmark-design: Section V-A, p.6: K_n,n with n = 40 to 120 in steps of 20, T = 100 trials per configuration. Note Table I lists only 60 to 120.
sinno-setup-hardware-software: Section V-A, p.6: Dell R705X, 128 logical cores, 503 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.10.9, Minorminer 0.2.16.
sinno-algorithm1-pseudocode: Appendix A, Algorithm 1, pp.8-9: inputs and outputs as listed, and lines 37-40 set J to 0 then J[a,b] = -1 for each pair in J coupling.

theory_low.qelm-test-variance-inverse-in-shots: Appendix A, p.13: one sentence says the variance is inversely proportional to N_test. No derivation is given and no condition is stated (independent shots are implied, not stated). A statement without proof, not a proved result.
theory_low.rqg-proposition-1: Section III, p.4, Proposition 1: the value adds that the approximation converges closer to the exact coefficient as ensembles grow. The paper states this informally; the appendix proves only the identity when each ensemble is the full set of subgraphs, with no rate or sampling-error bound. The text layer also garbles the statement's conditions.
